{{#title ESP32 ADC Non-Linearity Correction in Rust Using Lookup Table (LUT)}}

# ADC non-linearity issue in ESP32 

In the older versions of the ESP32 chip, like the one in the Devkit V1 (which you probably have too), there is non-linearity issue in the ADC. When I used the raw ADC value to calculate the temperature, I kept getting incorrect results. It confused me for a couple of days until I came across this article: [Using a Thermistor with Arduino and Unexpected ESP32 ADC Non-linearity](https://www.e-tinkers.com/2019/10/using-a-thermistor-with-arduino-and-unexpected-esp32-adc-non-linearity/). It explained the non-linearity issue with the ESP32's ADC.

The solution is to use a lookup table (LUT) to map the raw ADC value to a corrected one. However, the lookup table values vary from device to device because each ESP32 has a different internal reference voltage, so using it as-is might not work. This repository "[esp32-adc-calibrate](https://github.com/e-tinkers/esp32-adc-calibrate)" has the code to generate a custom LUT for your ESP32.

I ran the calibration program for my ESP32 and generated a lookup table (LUT) for my device. I have included that LUT below. It should work approximately for an ESP32 DevKit V1, but keep in mind that the ESP32 ADC characteristics vary from device to device, so the LUT is not guaranteed to be accurate for your board.

If you want to try generating a LUT specifically for your ESP32, I have included the calibration instructions at the bottom of this chapter. The calibration method is useful for improving the ADC reading, but it is still only an approximation. In my testing, using a LUT gives much better results than using the raw ADC value without any correction, but it does not make the temperature measurement perfectly accurate.

## Lookup Table 

We will be using this in our code to get the corrected one. 

Example usage:

```rust
let adc_value = 1900;
let corrected_adc: f64 = ADC_LUT[adc_value as usize]; // it will get you 2038.2
```


## Optional: Calibrate the ADC for your ESP32

If you want to generate a LUT for your own ESP32, you can try this approach:

### 1. Download the calibration program

Clone the calibration repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/e-tinkers/esp32-adc-calibrate.git
cd esp32-adc-calibrate
```

The repository contains a PlatformIO project that can be uploaded to the original ESP32.

### 2. Connect the DAC to the ADC

For the original ESP32 used by the DevKit V1, connect:

```text
GPIO25 (DAC) ---- GPIO35 (ADC)
```

Use a jumper wire for this connection.


### 3. Build and upload the program

First, install `uv` using the [official uv installation instructions](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/):

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

Verify the installation:

```bash
uv --version
```

Then build the project:

```bash
uvx platformio run
```

Upload it to the ESP32:

```bash
uvx platformio run -t upload
```

uvx runs PlatformIO in an isolated environment, so there is no need to install PlatformIO system-wide.


### 4. Open the serial monitor

The calibration program uses 500000 baud:

```bash
uvx platformio device monitor -b 500000
```

The program will print the generated LUT to the serial monitor.

### 5. Copy the generated LUT

Copy the complete LUT printed by the calibration program and replace the LUT in your Rust program with the one generated for your ESP32.
